newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mortgage-backeds ascend, but lag T-bond gains.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mortgage-backeds ascend, but lag T-bond gains.

text.p: Fueled by a benign inflation report early Thursday, U.S. Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities advanced to higher ground and largely clung to their gains much of the day, market sources said.
But Treasuries gained the upper hand in the rally as investors poured more funds into government bonds, causing pass-through yield spreads to widen by a whisker, they said.

Overall, producer prices had an unexpectedly strong 0.5 percent gain in December. But the meager 0.1 percent rise in the core number, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was more favorable for the markets.
Among pass-throughs, discount coupons rose furthest, up 12/32 to 13/32 by late Thursday afternoon.
Ginnie Mae 30-year 7.5 percent paper was up 12/32 at 99-31/32, yielding 102 basis points over 10-year Treasuries.
Comparable Fannie Mae issues were up 11/32 at 99-29/32, while Freddie Mac paper had gained 12/32 to stand at 100-03/32.
The 10-year note was up 20/32, yielding 6.50 percent.
Ginnie Mae and Fannie Mae prepayment reports, which are usually released on the fifth business day of the month, had soured the mood of many market players, traders said.
"With prepayments coming out in conventional 8.5s -- they were extremely high -- people started selling today," one New York trader said.
But one analyst said the jump in prepayments was an anomaly because the Freddie Mac prepayment report covers a different time period than those of Ginnie Mae or Fannie Mae.
"Interest rates change from the reporting period of prepayments for Ginnies and Fannies versus Freddies," explained a mortgage strategist.
She said refinancings would speed up only if the 10-year note yield dipped to 6.25 percent.
